AB-012.how:
Three reasons, in order of weight.

1. Not fixable as prescribed, because the clause has no on-disk existence. `grep -rn "Do not modify any file outside" .` returns exactly three hits, all of them the finding's own text: docs/audit/findings_merged.json:70 and :71, and docs/audit/findings/process.jsonl:9. There is no dispatch script, prompt template, or agent definition in the repo carrying the clause. It existed only as nine already-consumed Agent tool inputs; the nine workers terminated after writing docs/audit/findings/*.jsonl (mtimes 22:37 to 22:52 on 2026-08-19). Editing the quoted evidence would falsify the audit record rather than remove a constraint, since there is no live constraint left to remove.

2. It is not the failure the rule guards against. The DON'T INVENT JURISDICTION rule exists because an invented boundary later makes an agent decline work that was in scope. Here the boundary demonstrably suppressed nothing. Three findings in process.jsonl are about "$HOME/Library/Application Support/interstice-blocker-resolver/blocker_resolver.sh", a file entirely outside the repo, let alone outside docs/audit/findings/. AB-012 itself is a worker finding about the dispatching agent's own prompts. A boundary under which a worker freely audits the agent that wrote the boundary is not operating as jurisdiction; the workers read everything and reported everything.

3. It was load bearing, and it carried something the role sentence does not. "You do not fix anything" states a role, and a role is a thing a model reasons around at the margin ("this is a one-character typo, not a fix"). "Do not modify any file outside <dir>" is a mechanically checkable predicate over the filesystem. Nine workers ran concurrently, in one working tree, with no branch or git-worktree isolation, over a fifteen minute overlapping window. A single stray edit by any one of them would have been immediately visible to the other eight and to the main session, and would have silently moved the target the other eight were still measuring. Naming the one directory writes are permitted in is what keeps nine concurrent readers measuring the same repo. The auditor's own remedy, "State the role, not a territory", would trade a checkable predicate for an interpretable one at exactly the moment nine unsupervised writers share a tree.

No file changed. Rewording the historical record would be the only available edit and it would make the record less true.

AB-016.how:
Three reasons.

1. The prescribed fix is forbidden by the operator's own text. Item 0.7 of docs/GOAL_LOOP_STARS_READER_2026-08-17.md says to create the monitor "as a durable scheduled task via the Claude Code Remote MCP (create_trigger, cron */3 * * * * semantics as the server permits), not via the in-process CronCreate tools, which die with the session and would silently never run." The finding's fix is "Call CronCreate". Calling it would break an instruction the operator wrote, and by that instruction's own reasoning would produce a teardown that never fires, which is the exact failure the finding claims to prevent.

2. Two of the finding's three factual claims are false as of now. It says items 0.7 and 0.8 "both remain unticked"; both are `- [x]` today (ticked in commit 7db8e9e, "Loop notes and box ticks for this session", which landed after the worker wrote process.jsonl at 22:39). It says "no trigger id recorded in docs/STARS_NOTES_2026-08-19.md, so item Z8's teardown has nothing to delete by"; the notes carry a section headed "Identifier for teardown (item Z8, replacing 'trigger id')" giving the pid file path and the literal command, kill $(cat "$HOME/Library/Application Support/interstice-blocker-resolver/supervisor.pid"). Z8 has a handle, recorded in a committed file rather than in the session's memory, which is precisely what the rule wants.

3. The rule does not fit this process. "Auto-schedule follow-up for long-running background work" exists so that a result gets picked up and delivered instead of the user being asked to remember. The supervisor has no terminal result: its whole output is logs/blocker-ledger.md, appended every three minutes and consumed in-band by the loop while the loop runs. There is nothing to collect at an ETA, and the loop has no ETA, since it ends when its checklist is done rather than at a clock time. A one-time task at a guessed time would either fire early, killing a monitor item 0.7 explicitly requires to stay up "for the duration of this loop", or fire late and do only what Z8 already does. The finding's own fix concedes the regress it creates: the cron id would itself have to be recorded in the notes "so item Z8 can delete it", so the scheduled teardown needs the same manual teardown it was meant to replace.

The residual hazard the finding gestures at, an orphaned supervisor if the session dies before Z8, is answered by the same recorded handle: the kill command sits in a committed notes file, not in an agent's memory, so a later session or the user can execute it without this session. No file changed.

AB-017.how:
The repo root is now taken from the caller. "$HOME/Library/Application Support/interstice-blocker-resolver/blocker_resolver.sh" line 17 changed from R="/Users/scottlydon/Developer/interstice" to R="${1:-${INTERSTICE_ROOT:-/Users/scottlydon/Developer/interstice}}", with a WHY comment above it, so TALLY, LEDGER and WORKLOG all follow the caller's root. supervisor.sh now resolves the same way into ROOT and passes it through as the resolver's first argument.

The literal path stays as a last-resort default rather than becoming a mandatory argument (the finding suggested ${1:?usage}) because pid 82500 was already running and invokes the resolver with no argument; a mandatory argument would have made the monitor exit with a usage error every three minutes for the rest of the loop, breaking item 0.7. Both files were written to a temp path and moved into place with mv, so the rename could not disturb the descriptor the running bash holds open on supervisor.sh.

The install directory name still embeds the target ('interstice-blocker-resolver'). Renaming it would invalidate the teardown handle recorded in docs/STARS_NOTES_2026-08-19.md and the APP path the live supervisor resolved at launch, so it was left alone; the script itself, which is the thing that would be copied to a second loop, is now target agnostic.
